review:
Since I reviewed Gold Edition previously, I'm going to focus on the differences and new content here.  See my thoughts on why I enjoyed this game so much here http://steamcommunity.com/id/Soupinator/recommended/214770

Super Turbo Championship Edition is essentially a significant content DLC on top of Gold Edition, but since it makes so many changes to the game it is sold as standalone with a discount for previous owners.  Loading up a Gold Edition savegame simply would not work so if you started the game in Gold Edition you will have to start over in this one.  It adds two new large areas with new gameplay mechanics, adds a bunch of new enemy types (elite versions of existing enemies with new abilities,) some new graphical effects (heat distortion and shadows,) a new rage mechanic for combat, pollo bombs!, and reworks all the fights in the game.  There may be other changes I can't think of at the moment.

While none of the new content is strictly necessary to enjoy the game, I found it well worth the $5 upgrade.  The new areas are a lot of fun and quite unique compared to the rest of the game and are integrated seamlessly with the story.  The INTENSO rage mechanic works well as a panic button letting you recover from a fight that's going badly, and that does become necessary.  The fight rework in addition to the new enemies makes the game significantly more difficult which I appreciated but others may not.  In some fights they went a bit too far though, covering the screen with enemies, removing all sense of strategy and turning the combat into a spamfest.

So which version should you buy?  I would definitely recommend this one, with the caveat that you may find it too difficult.

Time for a trip to Mexico to become a luchador, save El Presidente’s daughter and become a legendary hero in Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition.

[h1]The Good:[/h1][i]Solid game all around. Nice treat having a Mexican setting to the game.[/i]

Alright, let’s get the obvious out of the way, this is an outstanding game. The gameplay is fluid, the soundtrack is catchy & memorable, the graphics are nice to look at (save for the risk of Epilepsy seizures), and the game’s price tag is good.

Another thing that should be noted is the fact that I can’t really recall another good game that had Mexican culture as it’s main premise. Nothing from what I saw looked out of place or out of line, and this game has lots of references, whether it’s from the visuals, like the various Nintendo items you’ll notice through your adventures, or the dialogue, like when you clear one area only to be greeted with the famous line “Your princess is in another castle.”

[h1]The Bad:[/h1][i]No significant difference between Normal & Hard modes.[/i]

Playing through both difficulty modes, I was rather disappointed by the lack of differences between the two. The enemies & bosses barely showed any difference, save for maybe more health; the checkpoints for the most part wasn’t changed or shortened; and not even the level design showed any changes. In general, hard mode is not hard.

[h1]The Ugly:[/h1][i]Missed potential for online co-op play.[/i]

Really, there wasn’t much that I could think of in terms of any other negatives for this game. The only other thing that I could think of, or in this case, looking at the other reviews done by the steam community, was noticing a lack of online co-op play.

Guacamelee! has had 2 additional versions of the game in Gold and Super Turbo Championship Editions and all of them, including the original, have a co-op option available. The latter version was a missed opportunity to try and make co-op gameplay available online.


Guacamelee! is a superb game, one that should be in anyone’s game collection. There’s little problems with the game itself that it gave me some difficulty in getting this review complete, but it’s done now and it gets an easy recommendation from me.

"Long" version:
[u]Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition[/u] or, from now on (for the sake of brevity), [u]Guacamelee![/u] is a 2D, metroidvania-side-scroller (is this even a thing?) developed and published by DrinkBox Studios. You take on the role of a luchador, with the objective of rescuing a damsel in distress from the grasp of an evil mafioso.

Let us discuss the story first.
While the game’s story might initially feel silly, with its countless goofy characters and their never-ending puns, the writing is solid and the developers managed to sneak in some heartfelt moments, which was surprising. The story is basically just going from A to B, pummeling everything in your way – it is simple but it works. There are also lots of pop culture references and little videogame and movie easter eggs (like Super Mario, for example). It is fun, but the novelty wears off about midway through the story.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3274631744
Gameplay is [u]Guacamelee![/u]’s focus and, thankfully, is enjoyable.
You start off with a few basic abilities, like punching and jumping, but you swiftly unlock new ones that allow you to deal with different enemies or make traversal easier or, in some cases, possible (many areas are inaccessible unless you have certain abilities).

Let us focus on exploration first.
Movement feels fluid and satisfying – the more abilities you unlock, the better it feels and the more freedom you have to deal with enemies and juggle them in the air.

Speaking of enemies, combat is up next. It is good, albeit a bit chaotic sometimes. It is very mashy, at first, but after unlocking new abilities that have certain colors associated with them, you will be introduced to new enemy types that have a colored shield, which requires a specific ability of said color to damage. Once you do that, you are free to damage the enemy as normal.

The combat sections only frustrated me one or two times, so I am totally OK with it, but the game introduced an enemy type or two that were either impervious to damage while charging at you or would barrel towards you way too fast, making it almost impossible to react accordingly. Now, I did get used to them, and would often try to cheese my way through each fight they were in, but they were never fun to deal with.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3274596989

While I liked the rhythm at which I unlocked new abilities, the farther I progressed through the story, the less I enjoyed the gameplay, as the maps became more complicated but not necessarily fun to traverse. Some of the abilities allow you to pretty much “fly” in a straight path, and those puzzles were also uninspired, I feel like. Also (and this is totally on me for doing it), trying to unlock everything is a chore.

In terms of graphics, [u]Guacamelee![/u] features a very colorful presentation that should exude charisma. I say “should” because, while I can see how most people would think of the game as having lots of personality, I still found it rather… bland.
It is not bad, by any means, but the more I played it the less impressive the new enemy design or the new environment looked.

When it comes to sound effects, the game is solid. Your hits carry impact and ambient noises are good.
There is no voice acting, as [u]Guacamelee![/u] relies on text-based dialogue to convey its story. The soundtrack is good, but I did find it a bit obnoxious from time to time (and yes, I did lower the volume).
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3274632213
I am unsure about this game, to be honest. It is definitely good and I can confidently recommend it on that basis; if asked whether I had lots of fun with it or would replay it, I would have to say no.

Again, a solid metroidvania with plenty of content. The price point is just right (and if you get it during a sale, even better!) and, by the looks of it, I am in the minority here. Most people love this game and you will most likely enjoy it too. It is just not my cup of tea, I guess.

Final score: 7 out of 10.

Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition is an upgraded version of Guacamelee, a metroidvania game inspired by Mexican culture. I already wrote a review for the original version, but this one deserves a review as well.

The story centers on Juan Aguacate, an agave farmer living in the outskirts of Pueblucho, a small Mexican town. During one Day of the Dead, an evil spirit who goes by the name of Carlos Calaca has a plan in mind for the worlds of the living and the dead. He kidnaps El Presidente's daughter (Juan's childhood friend and love interest), and kills Juan, who is then revived by a mythical Luchador mask. Juan then embarks on a quest across the worlds of the living and the dead in order to stop Calaca's plan, coming across many interesting characters along the way. The dialogue is pretty good, going from serious "we need to save the world" moments, to humorous jokes about the different characters, which still work very well.

The gameplay, like I mentioned in the opening paragraph, is that of a metroidvania platformer, with some combat mixed in. You start the game with a basic punch combo, and as you progress through the level you gain new moves as well as abilities, which then open up alternate paths in previous levels, leading you to new areas, or some hidden treasure. There's also a couple of "hub" levels, where you can get a few sidequests and also complete some bonus challenges. You can also unlock upgrades and costumes (which specific bonuses) using in-game currency, which is obtained when killing enemies. Talking about the enemies, there's a wide variety of them, from regular melee mooks, to flying enemies or giant, heavy hitting enemies.

Going into level design, it's pretty good. Plenty of large spaces to explore, with new areas that become available as you gain new abilities, which means you'll be revisiting areas all the time without feeling like they're repeating content. There's almost always something new to discover when the story sends you back to an already visited area. Also, the game uses a dual-world mechanic, with almost all levels having a World of the Living and World of the Dead version, and each version has its own unique aesthetic design; while the World of the Living is bright and colourful, the World of the Dead is dark and somber.

The soundtrack is top-notch. I'd say it's some kind of electro-mexican mix, and it fits the game very well. Not only that, but there's practically two versions of each song, since both worlds use their own music. While they share some similarities, there's differences in tone for the tracks of the World of the Living and the World of the Dead.

Now let's talk about the Super Turbo Championship Edition proper, in comparison to the Gold Edition. While the Gold Edition was already a pretty good game, the STCE (I'm not typing the full title again) adds two brand new areas to explore, several new enemy types, and a new boss, plus a couple of new abilities, including the Intenso mode, which allows you to tear through enemies with ease, plus some changes here and there. All in all, some pretty good content.

So, do I recommend Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition? Of course I do, it's a fantastic game, and if you enjoy metroidvanias, you'll really enjoy this one!

What is "Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition" ("Guacamelee")?

First of all, it is some years since I played this (in late 2014). Guacamelee is a Metroidvania game where you play a guy who is possessed by the spirit of a Luchador (Mexican wrestler) and must defeat enemies, overcome challenges, all the while learning new moves, finding some secrets, etc. in typical Metroidvania style.

Gameplay
The gameplay is very smooth, the challenging but never unfair difficulty makes it able to retry rooms without any issues - there is no death penalty other than having to restart the current room. This formula that is also used in Super Meat Boy etc. - getting right back into the game after failure - makes this game enjoyable until the end. You explore a world full of Mexican style, including some bonus levels in this version. Every now and then you meet some bosses to overcome, you can explore a small Mexican village, and with your powers gained throughout the game you defeat countless enemies, culminating in an optional (but necessary for achievements) pit of challenges. At the end of the game you will be the best Luchador in all of Mexico, but is this enough to break free of your destiny?
Minor spoiler: You can switch between the world of the living and the dead, reminiscent of the both greatest Zelda classics A Link to the Past and Majora's Mask, but you switch at any time - after having gained that power.

Story
The story is okay, but forgettable. If I remember it correctly, you die at the beginning and then try to resurrect. Or something like that. And some woman is also involved that you must rescue, I think. Or maybe just some chicken. Not sure anymore.
However, the characters are written in a fun style, and especially the chickens who teach you new moves are worth a laugh or two.

Controls
A controller is recommended, but with it controls are absolutely great. Everything is easily accessible except one special move that you use maybe once or twice in the game where you must press the joystick (you have to know this is even possible on the XBOX controller). I think it was used only once to solve a puzzle. Other than that, everything feels great. You can save at any point.
The negative point is that I think there is only one savegame.

Music
Are you even asking? The soundtrack is great, and I think I had also reviewed it. So read that review, or just listen to it on Youtube.

Hmm..
Naturally when you're looking to buy a game, you want to get the latest and greatest version. It should have all the extra content, bug-fixes, and so on. However, the possibility exists that the newest verson could be inferior in some ways. Game-design is a constant and always finicky, and nobody ever seems to be satisfied with its results. So things get changed, and changed again, sometimes they're even changed back to their original state. It's a constantly confusing nightmare, and for what? In the end it all comes down to preference.

Forgive me, I love to ramble.

STCE is on paper*, the superior version of Guacamelee! Let's look at some of the facts:

Two brand-new areas to explore!
A new boss-fight!
Intenso!
Multiple save-slots!
New enemies!
Every foe has a visible health-meter!
etc!

If you're hankering for more Guacamelee, then definitely grab this! The new areas are great. They make the world a bit richer, and are fleshed out with plenty of secrets and fighting/platforming to be had. I also like the little changes such as costumes being unlocked via silver coins. The biggest deal is that the controller-issue I had with Guaca-Gold is fixed, making this by default the superior version for me.

BUT!
STCE is a different game, and it can be considered inferior in a way. The controversial addition is Intenso! It's the "shock gloves"** of Guacamelee. Once you fill a meter you can become a superpowered luchadore by pressing L3+R3. Once you purchase all of the upgrades you're practically invincible. Guaca-Gold wasn't a difficult game, so having the ability to cheese the rare moments of challenge makes things a bit too easy. Keep in mind that this ability is optional. Most of the time I forgot I even had it. 

The new enemies are quaint. For the most part they're reskins that can move faster, hit (much) harder, and will sometimes teleport to get out of danger. Aside from nega-chupacabras doing tons of damage with their sword-stab, they're not a threat. There are also some flying fish in one of the new areas. They remind me of enemies from the Saturn version of Symphony of the Night. They only showed up in one area, and behaved in a similar manner. If it's a reference, then I applaud drinkbox for their attention to obscurity.

If you haven't played Guacamelee before, IMO it's best to go straight to this version. It's more convenient, since the original version doesn't have multiple save-slots. Having the most content is a definite plus as well. You might feel the urge to go back to Guaca-Gold for its original "true" level of difficulty but eh...I wouldn't recommend it. Most of Guacamelee's challenge is in a couple of boss-fights, and the optional areas like El Infierno. For the most part you're the awesome skull-cracking luchadore on a fun adventure. If you want a difficult Metroidvania, consider Valdis Story: Abyssal City (also on Steam).

Mostly though I'm just really happy and relieved that the controller issue I had with Guaca-Gold is fixed in this game. It's the main reason I'll probably never go back to the earlier version (though I have a fair number of achievements I should get).




*What is it with "on paper"? I use that phrase way too often.

**The gloves from Batman: Arkham Origins. Punch through any defense, combo count boost, makes things so easy.

When I was deciding which version to play, reading the comments gave me the impression that I should play both since the experiences were different and that I should finish both... which I did. Now, I can safely say that the Gold version is worth it only for 30 more achievements and nothing else. The STCE version improves almost everything that was lacking in Gold. Not to mention new mechanics, new levels, and extended duration. So yeah, if you want to play only one version, go with this definitive edition and don't look back.

[h1][u]The Short and Sweet[/u][/h1]
[u]Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition[/u] is a hybrid beat-em-up / Metroidvania game based on Mexican culture, with a large emphasis on combo-based combat, intelligent approach, and platforming. The story revolves around a farmer named Juan, who is killed by the main antagonist while attempting to save his friend, only to come back possessing the power of a magical mask, which turns him into a powerful Luchador intent on punching, suplexing and bodyslamming his way to victory.

As the player progresses through the game, they unlock more types of powerful attacks, such as large uppercuts and bodyslams, or utility abilities like clinging to or running up walls. Many of the combat abilities end up playing critical roles in platforming segments for their mobility, increasing the depth of the system. Additionally, some enemies can only be defeated by certain attacks, preventing the player from simply using brute force to make their way through any and all situations.

[b][u]Pros[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] The combat requires adaptability and precision from the player, making it a welcome challenge.

[*] Co-op with up to four players is supported, and is Steam Remote Play compatible.

[*] The art style and music is a pleasure to experience, both centered around Mexican culture.

[*] The combination of platforming and solid combat mesh well together, often overlapping for even more entertainment.

[*] The story and dialogue are entertaining throughout, and are definitely not a detriment to the experience.
[/list]

[b][u]Cons[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] Metroidvania’s style of backtracking can be a major turn-off for many players. Getting a lot of the upgrades requires backtracking, as does the “True Ending”. Both can rapidly become tedious if you choose to pursue them, but they are not necessary to complete the game, and can be ignored if desired. However, you are missing a large amount of content if you choose to do this.

[*] Playing with more than one player can quickly become absolute chaos during platforming, as the game has a few key mechanics that all players can control, but need to be precisely handled for successful platforming. Intense coordination can be required to surpass even the simplest of obstacles if playing with friends.
[/list]

[h1]Short Conclusion: Recommended[/h1]

[h1][u]In-Depth Analysis[/u][/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Guacamelee is a beat-em-up first and foremost. It primarily focuses on the combo system, encouraging the player to chain together as many hits as possible for the maximum amount of damage. This is fueled by the combo meter, a bar that shows the player how many times they can use their upgraded combat abilities before having to recharge. This, just like the health bar, is made larger by gathering upgrade pieces scattered across the game. 

Many enemies are coated in a colored shield that requires the player to use the matching ability on them in order to do damage. Multiple enemies can appear in a single area, each with a different shield color, and all shields eventually regenerate if not damaged for a few seconds, meaning Guacamelee expects the player to be a fast strategist and a good brawler. Combos are satisfying to pull off and deal large amounts of damage, helping to secure a kill before moving on to other enemies.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2114577601

The platforming is what you would expect from a platforming game, but gains extra depth with the implementation of the same abilities one would normally use for combos. A jump can be made higher with an uppercut, or longer with a dash. Many times a specific color-coded block requires a specific move to destroy, just like shields. This makes the platforming more enjoyable than the vanilla jump-n-climb every veteran gamer has become accustomed to by now.

Unfortunately, in order to unlock the “True Ending” of the game, the player must backtrack to reach multiple additional areas that are filled to the absolute brim with pure challenge platforming and combat. Two of them in particular are very, very time consuming and can be a major pain for players that don’t care much about challenge for the sake of challenge. I’ve been told [u]Guacamelee! Gold[/u] does not have these problems, as it was released before this edition, but as I have not played Gold or the original, I cannot speak on these problems.

 [h1]Story[/h1]
The story is entertaining in execution, but simple in overall plot. You are the hero going to rescue the girl. The player interacts with a wide variety of characters in this quest, some more interesting than others, and nearly all very entertaining to listen to. 
The game is absolutely riddled with comedy and references to other forms of media, making it almost worth playing for the story alone. But this story is merely the glue that holds all the combat and platforming together to form the Guacamelee experience.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
Guacamelee takes inspiration from Day of the Dead culture and Aztec designs to form a pleasing hybrid of rugged, chiseled shapes and decorated displays that I wholly enjoy looking at the entire time I am playing.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2114582753

The design of the game is very angular and sharp in nature, avoiding a lot of curves on important pieces. This strong and stylized form of art helps it to stand out among other games. The visuals are definitely a plus for Guacamelee.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Punches have impact and abilities give satisfying thumps, but the real winner of audio for Guacamelee is the music. Just like the art, it takes a heavy influence from traditional Mexican music, with a focus on guitars, trumpets, and vocals that are a joy to listen to. There’s just something about that combination of instruments and vocals that I can’t seem to get enough of. If you like mariachi music, like me, you’ll like Guacamelee’s music.

[h1]Technical[/h1]
[u]Specs:[/u] GeForce 840m 2GB, 8GB Memory, i7 CPU, Windows 8.1

I had zero problems running Guacamelee at 60fps, 1080p. However unlike most games, I experienced very noticeable and very annoying amounts of screen tearing with V-Sync turned off. Thankfully, the game is easy enough to run that turning on V-Sync had no impact on my ability to play at 60fps.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
While the Metroidvania nature may turn away some prospective gamers that dislike the focus on backtracking, most of the backtracking can be safely ignored if desired, allowing the player to focus solely on the solid combat / platforming gameplay, engaging story and culture-rich atmosphere. While it is perfectly fine solo, beware some gameplay complications if playing with a friend. 

Overall, at $14.99, I would say it is worth the price if you are a fan of the Metroidvania style, but it also goes on sale quite often at 50% or more. It is a competent game worthy of consideration by any player that finds these features exciting.

Guacamelee! is a game that I resisted playing for a long time, mostly because of my personal trauma with Metroidvanias. I have played in my life many games with Metroidvania aspects, such as Alien: Isolation and even Dark Souls. But few were the times I played those purebred 2D Metroidvania games - and those games really pushed my buttons. For you kids who weren't around back in the day, Metroidvanias were games that demanded a lot of memory and backtracking from players, making them aggravating for those of us who saw no fun in that.

But times changed, and much in the same way games perfected themselves to be more gamer-friendly, Guacamelee! shows that Metroidvanias too can catch up with more modern trends. And as such, it is the first true Metroidvania I truly loved. Of course there are still some aspects of it that brought me some PTSD - namely the treasure hunting. But for most part, it's an incredibly fun game, full of love from its developers.

For starters, as the title implies, this version of the game is expanded, adding a few things here and there. I never played the original version, but I can see playing the game as Tostada - originally a female NPC who appears at some cutscenes - is one of such additions. Now, when I describe this game as a Metroidvania, I pretty much describe about half of it: you gain powers as you progress, thus giving you access to areas that were previously inaccessible. But the game does a tremendous job in creating an unique identity for itself, which made it distinctive and celebrated in the Metroidvania appreciating community. 

The world can get quite big, but there's always a quest marker pointing you where to go. You're never lost on which direction to take, in that the game guides you to your next mission. The thing however - and this is where the game gets a bit clunky - is that to collect the previously locked treasures of an area, you have to backtrack and cover large distances to come and go. Thankfully, blocked paths appear on the map as squares with colours matching the move they need to be dis-obstructed. This lets you know where the places you couldn't access before are, thus facilitating things a lot. Plus, the game does have a fast travel system in form of these giant stone heads, and they are of enormous help to move around the world, yes. But still, you have to go to these stones to access the net of shortcuts, and it would have been much better - even for a matter of locomotion - if players could teleport to these heads from wherever they are. To aggravate things more, some locations don't have these heads. This is a massive blow against the game, since it affects so directly its treasure hunting aspect, making it not fun.

The combat however is the best aspect of the game. Being based in combos and dodging, it was actually fun to dispose of multiple enemies in an almost Arkham style. And the best part is that the powers you gain along the way become a direct part of combat: they're not there just to just open paths, and I saw myself incorporating them to combat. On top of that, you eventually get the Intenso, which is this power mode that makes you much more stronger, and charges with combat. Many times, you'll be locked in a room until you dispose of all enemies, and when you're done, a massive piñata will appear with a prize inside, letting you that bout ended.

Some enemies are your regular minions, while others move more quicker and dodge your attacks. And then there are the cursed ranged ones, tossing projectiles at you in the middle of a fight, or even during platforming, and they suck! As you progress, you'll find enemies who are more complicated, requiring different techniques: some enemies have shields with different colours, meaning that to break them, you have to hit them with the right move - but thankfully, Intenso can break any shield of any colour. Some enemies have multiple shields, and some enemies are shown as silhouettes, signalling that they're at another plan of reality, and you have to switch to fight them back.

Speaking of which, this is one of the most famous aspects of the game - the ability to traverse between the worlds of the living and the dead. Different worlds have their differences, such as platforms and barriers that appear and disappear. Many puzzles and fights demand quick inputs. Another power is to become a chicken, granting you access to smaller passages. This game is very much a platformer, and some platforming can be very tricky, specially at later levels. And remember that your powers are limited by a stamina-like bar, and that you can't perform the same fighting move more than once at a jump.

As you explore the world, you collect golden coins that you use to buy upgrades at checkpoints. Unfortunately, this is one of those games in which, once you buy everything, the gold starts pilling up. Then there are the purple coins, that you use to buy new costumes at the checkpoints. And these costumes have buffs and debuffs: they may grant you an advantage along with a disadvantage - you know how it is. Naturally, you'll also find upgrades for your health, stamina and Intenso capacities - they lie in chests, but you may also buy some of them. And there are even some side quests to be done, but don't expect quest marks for these ones.

Now, there are some elusive collectables that I recommend you to catch, which are the orbs. These things are incredibly well hidden - as in, you'll need walkthroughs for that crap. And once you find the hidden entrance for each of the orbs, you usually have to traverse a very demanding platforming section that will have you cursing at the devs. These orbs are hard to get, but once you do, you'll gain a fantastic power: the ability to fly freely as the chicken. This pretty much trivialises most of the other moves, and it's great for exploring. In fact, I suggest you to only go treasure hunting when you get that power. That's my advice: if you want to 100% this game, get the orbs as soon as you're able. Also, the orbs are important to get the real ending.

There's also the Pollo Bomb, which clears purple blocks, and it's not mandatory to get to the main boss. I kept on playing the game, believing that at some point I would be introduced to it like it had been happening with the other moves. But you get it in the Hell level, as a reward for completing a series of challenges. That wasn't very clear to me, but maybe it was my fault for not paying attention.

Last but certainly not least, the presentation. Guacamelee! is a gorgeous game, with a marvellous soundtrack to match (which also changes with the realities). The humorous dialogues, the character designs, the scenarios, everything is very pleasing to the eyes and ears. I find incredible that it took a group of Canadian developers to make one of the most wonderful love letters to Mexican culture that I know. But unfortunately... ugh, the pop culture references! The game is just littered with them! I admit that spotting the Me Gusta meme really brought me back to 2010. But most of it is just annoying as hell, and they dent what is otherwise a beautiful game. I mean, one of the moves is called Das Boot. Because when I'm playing a Metroidvania brawler themed after Mexican culture and folklore, I want to be reminded of 1980's German marine war movies.

In the end, Guacamelee! is not perfect in some aspects, but its highs go very high, thus deserving its classic status among Metroidvanias.

The game loads very fast. The story is quite engaging to keep you interested until the end, the NPCs and characters are funny and it has a lot of references to other video games and modern culture.

The platforming is quite fun, it's not the hardest but it has enough variance to keep you from getting bored after a while. I also like the use of different block types that you have to destroy from the bottom, top or the sides, it encourages the players to explore more areas to solve them, and they reward exploration well. There's always a prize every time you find a hidden corner somewhere. 

I don't use the map a lot but I really like that they have clear markers on things that I can discover within my area, a lot of other games don't even bother to do this and you ended up wasting time and find nothing in the area.

This game is quite combated heavy, there are variety of moves that you can chain to make combos and the combat is very satisfying. It's not the hardest but it keeps you engaged.

The  "normal" difficulty is quite balanced, although I found that the platforming is very forgiving, as an example, if you fell into the acid river it will just send you back to where you stand before, without any damage. I can't say I'm complaining because I failed a lot and definitely would have died a lot if it wasn't for this mechanic.

There are areas that feel like puzzles, since you can turn into little chicken to go through small areas, or travel to "other dimension" to make walls appear/vanish, and they are quite fun.

With that said, there are some complains I have about this game. The music is one, I just prefer 2D platforming with "calming" music since it sets the ambiance better for me. I had to turn down the music volume in this game just to feel that way.

But overall, Guacamelee is truly a gem and should be placed among the greatest Metroidvania games up there. I give it 9/10.

If there was ever a game that was part of that era of indie game that walked the well-treaded path that Braid braved first, but was still weighed down by the """humor""" of the early 2010s, it's Guacamelee. One of the first games to bring back and even being to solidify the sub-genre of "Metroidvania", Drinkbox Studios knew that they had to hit this out the park when they rolled this out. This being one of their first major releases (no one remembers Tales From Space), it was all or nothing, it would either make a splash and make ripples that would influence or fall flat on its face. Can we look back at this game and see confidently that this succeeded and accomplished all that it set out to do?

No, not at all, it's why I'm reviewing Super Turbo Championship Edition and not Gold/the Original.

It took Drinkbox Studio two times to make this game okay and most of that is due to the looks of the game and the sound of the music. The soundtrack is actually really good the more I think about it, it really has that driving force that pushes you along the game, always high energy, but never grating or tiring. The way this game looks is another mark for it, it's really lively, it's vibrant, no expenses were spared in the making of the stages, the characters, and the backgrounds. It's great.

I wish I can say the same about the gameplay. It's not horrible by any means, but I wouldn't call it particularly good either. It's all sorta limp and nebulous. When you can play on the hard mode of a game and make it out of the other side of the tunnel by basically doing the same combo over and over with maybe a headbutt/uppercut here or there to get past some of the move-specific shields, we got a problem. I did not change it up much during combat, no switch-up, no change, just straight oatmeal and I beat the game with little effort. Hell, most of my deaths was due to the platforming and lava pits which weren't even that big of a problem because this game gives you checkpoint after checkpoint. If the punishment for dying/failing is backtracking like 2-3 rooms, where is the excitement gonna come from? Why would I bother trying if the most Imma get is a slap on the wrist?

Another thing that bothered me about this game is the journey to 100%. If there is a genre that wants the player to get every thing, it's the metroidvania. A good metroidvania leaves bread crumbs for you, it litters the maps, the halls, rooms, walls, courtyards, and everything in between with these little goodies, the player wants them, but they can't get them. Yet. Progression is the name of the game here and nothing is better than getting an upgrade or item that makes your character better while also progressing the game forward. A double jump is useful. An uppercut is useful, especially when some enemies require an uppercut now. Same goes for a wallrun, a headbutt, a smash, a dash, a kick, the ability to shrink down, the ability to switch between realms on the fly. All these things are not only useful for traversal, the combat much more open, but the game begins to require these power-ups. You gotta use everything you got to win, to be the hero. To finally get that 100 fucking percent.

You wanna know what isn't useful or fun? Having to get gold medals in challenges in order to get an absolute dogshit egg bomb that has no other purpose other than exploding marked blocks. That's it. It doesn't make you better, it doesn't get you more movement, you can barely use it during combat and even when you do, it sucks. Why bother designing it like this? It's like the Balan Wonderworld costumes that do only ONE thing poorly for one section of the game. It's straight up ass.

Remember that humor I mentioned early? You wanna date your game? Put in a meme. Like, bro, you're telling me that an entire dev team looked at Business Cat and thought it was evergreen humor? For fuck's sake, one of your moves is called the Dashing Derpderp. C'mon man, even back in 2014, we were better than this.

Guacamelee is a pretty package, gently tied in a bow, wrapped with care. It's a shame that the only things inside it are 99 cent wrestler toys that smell weird, tamarindo candy wrappers and Michaels Dia de los Muertos made in china plastic skulls.

I enjoy Guacamelee! overall. Its primary focus is on beat-’em-up combat and platforming, and it blends those two elements well. The combat is satisfying, especially with how you can stagger enemies and throw them into each other to control crowds. It’s fast, punchy, and feels great once everything clicks.

[h2]Gameplay & Platforming[/h2]
The inputs can feel a little stiff, which means you need to be very precise—especially during platforming sections. For simply completing the main story, this isn’t a big problem, and most of the platforming is fairly smooth. But if you’re going for secrets or optional challenges, some of those areas can be surprisingly demanding and occasionally frustrating.

[h2]Story & Pacing[/h2]
I’m not a fan of the story interruptions. They’re mostly front-loaded, but they still break the pacing early on. Once the game settles into its rhythm, though, the focus shifts back to what it does best: combat and platforming.

[h2]Exploration[/h2]
I appreciate that the game clearly marks objectives and generally keeps you moving forward. I like this direction-focused approach, though others may find it makes the game feel more like an action-platformer than a true Metroidvania. If you enjoy wandering and getting lost in a big interconnected world, Guacamelee! might feel a little too guided. But if you just want solid combat, tight movement challenges, and clear progression, it’s a great fit.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Overall, Guacamelee! is one of the better Metroidvanias. It has fun combat, memorable movement challenges, and a strong sense of style. Some rigid inputs and pacing hiccups hold it back a bit, but as a whole, it’s an excellent game.

It's....okay. I think this game is like, the perfect candidate for a "Maybe" recommendation tag on Steam. I've bought both this and the older Gold Edition and probably have 20 hours as a whole across them both and I've bounced off them each time. 

The core gameplay is fun: grappling and throwing enemies around, including into other enemies is a neat twist on the usual combat for these kinds of games. The graphics are colorful and vibrant. The music is catchy. It's not terribly long or the sort of game that pads out its runtime. Some of the dialogue can be funny. 

It's also the sort of game that trades story for gaming references and jokes that are kind of run into the ground like an episode of Family Guy. I would've appreciated a little more story or worldbuilding for as colorful as the world is, it's mostly a vehicle to give "hey I recognize that thing"-style references to other video games. This doesn't always have to be a dealbreaker, but in a Metroidvania you should want to explore the world because that's a big part of the genre's concept and Guacamelee's world isn't...interesting enough on its own to want to explore. 

It's also kind of exhausting to play: by the end, the final dungeon, once all the mechanics are unlocked, enemies have a laundry list of things you have to do to be able to kill them (gotta be in the right dimension, gotta attack them with the right color attack, gotta dodge X and Y attack, but you can't dodge Z, etc) and the fights themselves turn into chaotic clusterfucks once 3+ enemies are on the screen where the action can be difficulty to follow and I just wasn't having much fun with the core combat anymore. The mechanics seem to build on in a way that's there to make it harder to kill enemies rather than to create any kind of fun variations on the core combat loop, such as giving them the ability to teleport away from you mid-combo to break up your all-important combo stack or the ability to be immune to all damage except certain attacks. 

And then little problems like some really questionable hit detection or a boss bugging out and changing attacks mid-animation, etc.

It's also a really platforming-heavy game with some puzzles that require precise timing and a section midway through the game (the volcano) where they throw in a lot of instant-death mechanics that just...grate.

So...it's a "maybe" game. Maybe it can be a game you really dig, if the above doesn't really bother you. I'd wait for it to go on sale.

Edit: my review of the old Guacamelee version still applies, but also could in mind that I felt this version felt like a whole new game. Make of that what you will.

I recommend this game as a Metroidvania, though it is quite short. If you are looking for something longer, you should probably play Silksong. Overall, the game is really beautiful, and the story is legendary. I loved how it features two different endings that completely change future events, though I definitely prefer the second ending over the first one.

Pros
Excellent Story: The plot is very well-done and highly engaging.

Combat & Progression: Great variety in combat moves, how you unlock them, and how they are ordered throughout the game.

Dimension Swapping: The mechanic of shifting between the World of the Living and the World of the Dead is an absolute blast and adds amazing variety.

Decent Music: The soundtrack is nice and fits the theme well.

Cons
Too Easy: The game is incredibly easy, to an unnatural degree. Even the final boss was a complete walk in the park.

Technical Issues: The game has annoying bugs with the save system, and it randomly crashes, kicking you out in the middle of gameplay.

Conclusion
In conclusion, I hope the second installment is even better, as I am planning to play it next and will drop my review once I finish it. Huge thanks to the development team for creating this game!
